A perusal is the act of reading something. When you sit down and read through a document, a letter, a report, or any piece of writing, that act of reading — that experience of going through the text — is called a perusal.

Simple example:

"She gave the contract a perusal before signing."

→ She read through the contract.
The important nuance: careful vs. quick

This is the most important thing to understand about this word, because it has two coexisting meanings, and knowing both will protect you from confusion.

Meaning 1 — Careful, thorough reading (the traditional and formal meaning):
Originally, a perusal meant a careful, attentive, detail-oriented reading of something. The kind of reading where you're absorbing every word, examining things closely.

"After a thorough perusal of the evidence, the judge delivered her verdict."

→ The judge read through it carefully and attentively.

Meaning 2 — A quick, casual scan (the modern everyday meaning):
Over time, people started using "perusal" to mean almost the opposite — a light, brief, passing glance through something, like quickly flipping through a magazine.

"I gave the menu a quick perusal and ordered the pasta."

→ A fast, casual look — not a deep study.

Both meanings are real and used today. Because of this, when you use the word yourself, pair it with a describing word to avoid confusion:

  • "careful perusal" or "close perusal" → thorough reading
  • "quick perusal" or "brief perusal" → casual scan

Fair question. The difference is in tone and weight.

"Reading" is plain and neutral. "Perusal" carries a sense of purpose and deliberateness — it suggests you're examining something that actually deserves attention. It also sounds more formal and polished.

This is why you'll almost always see "perusal" used with things like documents, contracts, reports, files, manuscripts, or letters — not with a comic book or a WhatsApp message.
The most common phrase: "for your perusal"

You will encounter this phrase a lot, especially in professional and formal writing. It simply means "so that you may read it" — you're handing something over for someone to look through.

"Please find the revised proposal attached for your perusal."

→ Here, read this. Look it over.

It's a polite, slightly formal way of saying "here it is — take a look." You'll see it in business emails, legal correspondence, and formal letters constantly.

Other common phrases:

  • "upon perusal" = after reading it → "Upon perusal of the file, he noticed several mistakes."
  • "a perusal of" = a reading of → "A perusal of the records showed inconsistencies."
The feel and register of the word

"Perusal" is a formal word. It belongs in:

  • Business and professional emails
  • Legal and official documents
  • Academic writing
  • Literary or serious prose

You would not use it in casual speech. You wouldn't say to a friend, "Give my text message a perusal." That would sound strange and stiff. In everyday conversation, you'd just say "read this" or "take a look."

But in writing — especially any professional context — it's a perfectly natural and respected word.

Think of perusal as the formal, purposeful cousin of "reading." It's what you do when you sit down and go through something that matters — whether that's a careful read or just a quick scan, depending on context. The word signals that you're not just idly glancing; there's some intentionality behind it.

If someone hands you a document and says "please take it for your perusal," they are politely inviting you to read it and form your thoughts. That's the word's soul: reading with some degree of purpose and awareness.
